title: Let the guest be a god
hookLine: a teacher sends his student into life, and his parting words put the guest beside mother, father and teacher
carry: atithidevo bhava: welcome the guest as god
tomorrow: how big is a family, in two Sanskrit words?

cards: Somebody new is coming over this week: a friend's partner, a neighbor, a classmate who's never seen the house. The cushions get fluffed. The snacks get serious.

In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher has finished teaching his student the Veda, and the student is about to leave for the life of a householder. So the teacher gives him his parting words. Speak the truth.
Live by dharma. Don't stop learning. And then four short lines, the last of them this: atithidevo bhava.
Let the guest be a god to you.

teach.b: The four lines run: matridevo bhava, pitridevo bhava, acharyadevo bhava, atithidevo bhava. Let your mother be a god to you. Your father.
Your teacher. Your guest. Notice the order.
It starts with the people who raised you, then the one who taught you, and only then opens the door to someone you may never have met. And look at the guest's name.
Atithi is often explained as a-tithi: one with no fixed date. The guest who didn't book a day, who simply turns up. That's who is set in the same row as your parents.
In the sound, the -ah of atithidevah turns to o before bhava, in all four lines. Now here's why the line runs so deep in Hindu homes.

teach.h: PUJA: GOD WELCOMED AS A GUEST.
teach.b: When Hindus do puja, they welcome God the way you'd welcome an honored guest: a seat is offered, water for the feet, water to sip, then food, flowers and light.
The old lists of offerings read like a host's checklist.

teach.h: LET THE GUEST BE A GOD TO YOU.
teach.b: So the teaching runs both ways. Worship is hospitality to God, and hospitality is a kind of worship. The glass of water handed to someone at the door is the same gesture made at the shrine.
Not a stranger to be put up with: someone to honor, fed first, given the best seat.

how: In puja, many Hindus offer a deity the welcome given an honored guest: a seat, water, food, flowers and light; at home, atithidevo bhava is taken as a rule of hospitality, with the guest offered water, food and the best seat first.

o: the changes sounds make where words touch
an old phrase for setting a table for guests
a list of the people a student must obey

games.q: the guest line, taken apart — tap the pairs.
p: a guest: often read as one with no fixed date
God welcomed like an honored guest

s: atithidevo bhava is a modern tourism slogan
it's from the Taittiriya Upanishad, among a teacher's parting words to his student.
puja offers God a guest's welcome: a seat, water, food, light
worship is hospitality to God; the line makes hospitality a kind of worship.
the four lines honor teachers only
mother, father, teacher and guest, each in the same pattern.

games.q: a friend at your house notices your mom offers the shrine water and food, then offers her the same, in the same order. she asks if that's a coincidence. what do you say?
o: no: puja welcomes God like an honored guest, and atithidevo bhava welcomes a guest like God.
yes: it's just the order the kitchen runs in.
it's so the guest knows the food was blessed first.
games.why: the welcome at the shrine and the welcome at the door are the same gesture. the Taittiriya sets the guest in the row of mother, father and teacher.

practice: If you keep a shrine, offer a little water or food there before your next meal, as many Hindu homes do, and notice it's the same welcome you'd give a guest.
If you don't, picture the next person likely to come through your door, and one small welcome you could have waiting: a clear chair, a glass of water, your phone put away.
Hold that picture, and let the breath slow around it, as if you were already listening for the knock.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: sounds changing where words meet. Today, atithidevah becoming atithidevo before bhava: the guest, a god.

orig.note: Sanskrit: let the guest be a god to you (Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2).

carryVoice: Worth keeping: atithidevo bhava, welcome the guest as god, the same welcome God gets at the shrine. See you tomorrow.
